games.explanation: Detroit at this number assumes Framber Valdez is going to do Framber Valdez things against a lineup that actually matches up fine with him. Washington runs a left-handed heavy top of the order featuring James Wood, and Valdez has been noticeably more hittable against lefties than the reputation suggests. The Tigers are also pricing this like they've got a real edge on the mound, but 1453 to 1448 is a coin flip dressed up in pinstripes, and getting plus money on a coin flip is the entire game. Lovelady is the obvious wart, but a Comerica night game with the wind blowing in at 11 mph keeps the margin for error wider than the board thinks. +154 on the actual toss-up is the pitch.

The market is still pricing the Yankees like it's April, when the actual gap between these two clubs has quietly closed to nothing. Tampa runs out the better lineup against right-handed pitching tonight, with Aranda and Caminero doing real damage on that side and Díaz anchoring things at a .353 xwOBA. The wind blowing in at 11 mph takes the Yankee power bats down a rung in a park that otherwise plays homer-friendly, which is exactly the environment Seymour's fly-ball, high-whiff profile wants. Getting a coin flip at +133 is the pitch, and the Rays are closer to the coin flip than the board thinks.

Chris Sale against a lineup stacked with lefty-mashing righties is exactly the kind of matchup the board keeps refusing to price correctly, because the name still commands a discount that his splits don't justify. Sale's numbers against left-handed bats are noticeably softer than the topline suggests, and Cincinnati happens to trot out Myers, Stewart, and Stephenson, all of whom do their real damage against southpaws. Abbott isn't Sale, but he's been perfectly competent, and the projected margin here is half a run in a neutral park with harmless wind. At +220 on a dog our model gives a better than one-in-three shot, you're getting paid twice over for a game that profiles as a coin flip with a tilt.

The market keeps treating the Angels like the house team in this rivalry, and it keeps being wrong about what that actually means. Springs isn't overpowering, but he's steady enough to keep a lineup that leans on Trout and Neto from running away with anything, and the A's have the more coherent stack top to bottom. Butler and McNeil have been the kind of contact-plus-thump profile that quietly wins tight road games, and this projects to be exactly that, a one-run scrap where the coin flip is closer to 55/45 than the board suggests. Getting +116 on the better team by a small but real margin is the whole reason to be here.

Yamamoto is the better pitcher, nobody's arguing that, but a coin flip is not what this line is selling. San Diego runs out a top of the order that hits righties as hard as anyone in the division, and Tatis and Machado both bring roughly .370 xwOBAs into a park that quietly plays as one of the best homer environments in the league. Ray's walks are the obvious wart, but Ohtani aside, this Dodgers lineup isn't the murderers row the price implies. Getting +185 on a game our numbers see closer to a pick means the market is paying Yamamoto's reputation tax, and we're happy to collect the other side.
